summary: Defines BRSKI with Alternative Enrollment, which extends BRSKI to support certificate enrollment mechanisms other than the originally specified Enrollment over Secure Transport. It supports enrollment protocols such as CMP.

eli5.summary: A new device joins a network and gets its ID card. This lets the ID card be issued by other methods than the original one.

questions: brski with enrollment other than est
why not use est for brski
what is the brski-reg-cmp service name
subtitle: How a new device can get its domain certificate through enrollment protocols other than EST, such as CMP.

tldr.problem: BRSKI normally enrolls a new device's certificate with EST, which cannot carry proof of who sent a request across several hops and does not suit every device, key type or site.
tldr.mechanism: BRSKI-AE lets the registrar offer enrollment protocols whose requests are authenticated self-contained objects, such as CMP, carried over the same TLS channel and addressed by a generalized well-known URI.
tldr.outcome: A registrar can act as a local registration authority and pass the device's signed request on to a backend RA and CA, while the voucher and status steps stay as in BRSKI.

today: RFC 9733 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on RFC 8995.

sections.title: What BRSKI-AE Changes
sections.content:
RFC 8995 defines BRSKI, a way for a new device (the pledge) to join a network. It is typically used with Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST, RFC 7030) to obtain a certificate for the device. BRSKI-AE is a variant that uses other enrollment protocols whose requests are authenticated self-contained objects.

It keeps the main ideas of BRSKI. The pledge arrives with an IDevID credential installed by its manufacturer. It uses a voucher exchange to obtain a trust anchor for the domain. It then generates a private key and asks the domain PKI, through the registrar, for a domain-specific LDevID certificate.

The RFC also extends the well-known URI structure with a path element naming the enrollment protocol, and lets the registrar offer several protocols. With its referenced documents, the specification is sufficient to run BRSKI with the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) as profiled in RFC 9483.
sections.eli5: A new gadget has a factory ID and wants a local ID for the network it joins. This document lets the gadget ask for the local ID in more ways than before.

sections.title: Scenarios That Need Alternatives
sections.content:
The RFC lists situations where EST is a poor fit:

  • Pledges or the target domain already use another protocol such as CMP.
  • The registration authority (RA) is not next to the registrar and needs end-to-end authentication of the requester, which EST does not provide over several transport hops.
  • The RA or CA operator wants auditable proof of origin for certificate signing requests, which TLS cannot give because it offers only transient source authentication.
  • Certificates are wanted for key types, such as Key Encapsulation Mechanism keys, whose proof of possession needs a fresh challenge value rather than a single message.
  • The pledge's security libraries lack EST support or the tls-unique value that EST requires.
  • Full RA functionality is not on site and the link to an off-site RA may be intermittent or offline.

Appendix A gives industrial examples such as rolling stock, building automation, substation automation and electric vehicle charging.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the helper who approves the ID card is far away or only reachable now and then. The request has to carry its own signature so it stays trustworthy while it travels.

sections.title: Proof of Possession and Proof of Identity
sections.content:
A certification request must carry two properties. Proof of possession shows access to the private key matching the public key in the request, typically by a self-signature. Proof of identity, also called proof of origin, authenticates who sent the request, typically by a signature made with the pledge's IDevID secret over data that includes a strong identifier such as the device serial number.

A PKCS #10 or CRMF request signed with the new key gives integrity and proof of possession, but not identity, because the new key pair has no confirmed identity yet. The RFC reviews how existing protocols handle identity. EST binds the request to the TLS session through tls-unique, which outside parties such as a second RA cannot verify. SCEP, CMP and CMC protect requests with a shared secret or an existing certificate, so they do not rely on the transport.

The RFC concludes that EST does not meet the requirements for authenticated self-contained objects, but SCEP, CMP and CMC do, and it focuses on CMP.
sections.eli5: The request has to show two things: that you really own the new key, and that the old factory ID vouches for you. A signature from the factory ID does the second job.

sections.title: Architecture and the Registrar's Role
sections.content:
The core rule is that authorization of a certification request MUST be based on an authenticated self-contained object tied to the IDevID credentials. Because the request is self-contained, it may be transferred by any mechanism.

The architecture has the same logical elements as BRSKI: pledge, join proxy, domain registrar, the MASA and ownership tracker, plus an RA and a CA in the PKI. The registrar can still do all checks, or it can act as a Local Registration Authority (LRA) and forward requests to a backend RA. The registrar MUST support at least one enrollment protocol with authenticated self-contained objects.

If the registrar forwards requests, it cannot use a different enrollment protocol toward the PKI than the one used with the pledge, because the pledge's signed request must be upheld end to end. The certificate enrollment messages are REQUIRED to travel over the (D)TLS channel already set up between pledge and registrar, so the registrar keeps full control of the enrollment traffic.
sections.eli5: The front-desk helper (the registrar) can approve a request itself or pass it on to a head office. Either way, the original signed request must arrive unchanged.

sections.title: The Message Exchange
sections.content:
The pledge behaves as in RFC 8995 with one exception: after the Imprint step, the Enroll step MUST use an enrollment protocol with authenticated self-contained objects. Discovery, the voucher exchange and voucher status telemetry stay as in BRSKI, and the final enrollment status telemetry is kept as a separate phase.

Within enrollment, only the certification request and response are REQUIRED. The others are optional: a CA certificates request and response, an attribute request and response, and a certificate confirm with a PKI or registrar confirm. Certificate confirmation is not supported by EST but is by CMP.

For each request the registrar may answer directly, in which case it MUST sign its answer with the credentials it used for TLS during the voucher exchange, or it MUST forward the request to the RA. It could answer CA certificate or attribute requests from a cache or from provisioned data, and it can reject a bad certification request itself.
sections.eli5: Only one back-and-forth is a must: the request and the answer. Asking for extras and saying thank you afterwards are optional.

sections.title: Endpoint Addressing
sections.content:
BRSKI addresses EST functions with URIs such as /.well-known/est/simpleenroll. BRSKI-AE generalizes this to /.well-known/<enrollment-protocol>/<request>. The protocol component MUST name the protocol in use, for example est or cmp. A new protocol needs its values specified in a suitable RFC and placed in the Well-Known URIs registry.

A pledge SHOULD use the endpoints defined for the protocols it supports. It finds out whether the registrar supports a request by sending it and checking the HTTP status code. The RFC's example registrar lists the BRSKI endpoints voucherrequest, voucher_status and enrollstatus, several EST endpoints, and the CMP endpoints getcacerts, getcertreqtemplate, initialization and pkcs10.
sections.eli5: Each kind of request has its own mailbox address, and the address starts with the name of the method you use. The registrar's reply tells you whether it has that mailbox.

sections.title: BRSKI-CMP
sections.content:
The RFC defines CMP as the normative instantiation. Adherence to the Lightweight CMP Profile (RFC 9483) is REQUIRED. The pledge's CMP client MUST validate responses against the trust anchor from the voucher, the pinned-domain-cert. Proof of possession fits the key type, and proof of identity is a signature over the request using the IDevID secret.

When the registrar forwards a request, it is RECOMMENDED to wrap the original request in a nested message signed with its own credentials. That conveys its consent to the RA while keeping the pledge's signature. Extra trust anchors SHOULD be delivered in the caPubs field of the certification response. Delayed delivery follows RFC 9483 for asynchronous channels.

CMP can also be combined with Constrained BRSKI using CoAP transfer (RFC 9482). Where no general discovery exists, a minimalist approach uses the service name brski-reg-cmp instead of brski-registrar, though that does not support join proxies. CMC, SCEP and EST-fullCMC are left for future work.
sections.eli5: The document picks one concrete method, CMP, and spells out exactly how to use it. Other methods may be added later.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8995 apply. The key extra concern is that even when the registrar hands its RA role to a separate system, it must still take part in deciding whether a pledge joins, so a pledge cannot bypass it to get an LDevID certificate. The RFC lists ways to do this: implicit consent, out-of-band signaling such as entering the pledge identity in a database, an extra message on the same channel, or the registrar signing the enrollment request in addition to the pledge.

On privacy, CMP messages themselves are not encrypted. Eavesdroppers could learn which devices are being bootstrapped, and might selectively block some. TLS already protects the pledge-to-registrar leg, while the onward exchange with backend systems may need encryption added.
sections.eli5: Even if a far-away office issues the ID card, the local front desk must still say yes first. And since the paperwork is not secret by itself, it should travel in a sealed envelope.
